name: Lash extensions

card.summary: Salon-applied individual lashes bonded to your own for length and fullness, lasting a few weeks per set.
card.note: Adhesive fumes have been linked to respiratory problems in technicians.

quick.overview:
Lash extensions are individual false lashes glued onto natural lashes by a technician. They add length, curl and density and last roughly three to four weeks.

Styles range from natural-looking classic sets to fuller volume sets.
quick.mechanism: Each synthetic lash is attached to a single natural lash with cyanoacrylate-type adhesive, and falls out as the natural lash sheds.
quick.risks: A case report linked the glue to occupational asthma and rhinitis in technicians. Licensing rules vary by jurisdiction. Few clinical studies examine client outcomes.

lead: Lash extensions are individual synthetic (or sometimes natural-material) lashes attached by a technician to a person's own lashes with semi-permanent adhesive, to add length, curl and fullness. According to Wikipedia, an application typically takes up to two hours and lasts about three to four weeks depending on care [1]. For appearance, the result is a fuller, darker lash line that frames the eyes without daily mascara or strip lashes.

Styles are commonly described as classic (the most natural), volume (the fullest) and hybrid (a mix). The technician customises material, length, colour and curvature to the client's eye shape, lids and natural lashes [1]. This distinguishes extensions from temporary strip lashes and magnetic lashes, which the wearer applies and removes herself or himself [1].

The adhesives commonly contain cyanoacrylate, and published case reports have linked the fumes to occupational asthma and rhinitis in lash technicians [2]. The American Academy of Ophthalmology lists allergic reaction, infection and lash loss among the risks to clients [4].

angle.text: A technician adds lashes to the natural ones to give a fuller, longer lash line for weeks at a time, with the style chosen to suit the eye shape.

infobox: Varies by US state; some require cosmetology or lash-specific licences [1]

paras: Temporary strip lashes are synthetic strips trimmed to fit and attached above the natural lashes with temporary glue; they come off with warm water or makeup remover and are not meant for showering, sleeping or swimming. Magnetic lashes sandwich the natural lashes between magnetic layers [1]. Extensions are applied lash by lash with semi-permanent glue [1].

Artificial lashes predate extensions. A 1882 report described Parisians sewing hair into lids, Karl Nessler patented artificial lashes in the UK in 1902 to 1903 and sold them in London, and Anna Taylor patented a design in the US in 1911 [1]. D. W. Griffith had human-hair lashes fitted to actress Seena Owen for Intolerance in 1916, false lashes became popular in the early 1930s, and Twiggy helped popularise the doll-like lash look in the 1960s [1]. Katy Stoka invented magnetic false lashes in 2014 [1].

Extensions are bonded to individual natural lashes using instant glue. Specialist equipment exists for the work, including a patented hands-free low-pressure air source with a finger-mounted nozzle designed to direct airflow during application [3].

A 2013 report in Occupational Medicine described a case of occupational asthma with rhinitis and a case of rhinitis attributed to cyanoacrylate-based lash extension glue among beauty professionals, noting that the number of practitioners was increasing [2].

The American Academy of Ophthalmology reports that the glue can cause pain, itching, redness and swelling and that some glues have contained formaldehyde. It also lists infection and eye injury from unhygienic salons or sharp tools, and temporary or permanent lash loss from tugging. Its guidance includes choosing a trained technician, asking for the ingredient list and requesting a spot test, and seeing an ophthalmologist for reactions instead of removing the lashes oneself. It notes the FDA does not regulate lash extensions or their glue [4]. Wikipedia notes magnetic lashes may pose a hazard in MRI rooms [1].
No studies found on the effect of lash extensions on appearance. Published literature includes a case report of occupational respiratory disease in technicians exposed to the adhesive [2].
